$comment: Pinned repo-side contract for the controls that would otherwise trust a
repository-controlled artifact at its word.
The rubric invokes package.json scripts, reads facetheory.lesser.json, and runs a
named set of security tests. Every one of those is editable in the same pull
request as the change being gated, so 'the command exited 0' is not by itself
evidence: a script rewritten to `true` exits 0, an emptied test file exits 0, and a
retargeted manifest path exits 0. This file is the expected value each of those
controls asserts against.
What this does buy: a bypass can no longer hide inside an application-shaped file.
Stubbing `pnpm run build` now requires editing gov-infra/planning in the same diff,
at the governance boundary, where the change is the review's subject rather than
incidental. What it does NOT buy: this is not a cryptographic binding, and an
author who edits both sides can still move the pin. The control it composes with is
cross-client adversarial review of the gov-infra diff, not this file alone.
Command text is not behaviour. `validate:csp` pinned to `node scripts/audit-csp.mjs`
holds perfectly while that file is emptied, and SEC-4 then exits 0 having audited
nothing. So the pins below reach content: every executable this rubric runs, and
every probe it counts, is bound by SHA-256 rather than by the string that names it.
Changing any value here is a governance change. It travels with the reason, in the
commit that needs it, and never as drive-by maintenance. Duplicate keys are rejected
when this file is read: JSON.parse is last-wins, so a repeated key is a value a
reviewer reads and a different value a control enforces.
Exact expected text of every script the rubric's exit-code trust depends on,
including the transitive closure reached through `pnpm run`. CON-5 asserts each
pinned script matches byte-for-byte, and that no pinned script delegates to a
script outside this map — a sub-script is otherwise a hole under a pinned parent.

expected.build:assets: node scripts/copy-facetheory-manifest.mjs && node scripts/build-stylesheet.mjs && node scripts/copy-brand-assets.mjs
expected.build: pnpm run typecheck && pnpm run svelte-check && pnpm run build:client && pnpm run build:server && pnpm run build:assets && pnpm run validate
expected.validate: pnpm run validate:renderer-authority && pnpm run validate:csp

$comment: The content of everything the guarded scripts above actually execute. CON-5 walks
the closure — each `node <path>` target, each file a listed glob expands to, and
each relative module those files import, transitively — and asserts a SHA-256 for
every member. A target with no pin fails; a pin no command reaches fails too, so
this map stays exactly the closure instead of drifting into a wish list.
`unpinned_import_roots` is the declared boundary of that walk. `src/` is the
application the probes are written against: hashing it would freeze the subject
under governance and invert the relationship, because the probe is the gate and the
module is what it judges. `build/` is generated output — regenerated every run, and
asserted by COM-1 and driven by SEC-6 rather than pinned. A gate that imports helper
logic out of either root is a limit recorded in the threat model, not a hole this
map closes.
`allowed_globs` is the set of glob arguments a guarded `node` invocation may pass.
Every file a listed glob expands to still has to be pinned; the list exists so a
new glob is a governance edit rather than a silent widening.
`node gov-infra/verifiers/check-package-scripts.mjs --print-hashes` prints this map
for the current tree, so a legitimate move is mechanical rather than hand-computed.
`build.command` is what `lesser client install` executes. An allowlist of exact
invocations is the only form of this check that means anything: any non-empty
string array satisfies a shape check, including one that runs something else
entirely. Path keys are validated structurally (no absolute path, no `..`,
resolved beneath the repository root, entry beneath the server dir) rather than
pinned, so the layout can move without a governance edit while containment holds.
SEC-6's inventory. `node --test <files>` exits 0 on a file containing no tests,
so existence is not coverage. Each file below must be present and must report at
least `min_test_points` passing TAP test points (TAP's own name for the ok/not ok
assertions a run emits, counting nested subtests). Deleting a test, emptying a
file, or dropping one from the invocation all fail the control.
The minimums sit at the current counts. They ratchet up with new coverage and
are lowered only with a stated reason — lowering one is how coverage is retired,
and it is meant to be visible when it happens.
A count is still not coverage: sixteen assertions that assert nothing satisfy a
minimum of sixteen, and one probe symlinked to another satisfies two entries from
one file. So each entry pins the probe's SHA-256 as well, symlinked probes are
rejected on lstat, and two entries naming one path are rejected outright.
The hard boundary is that no install in this rubric or in CI runs lifecycle
scripts: every `pnpm install` carries `--ignore-scripts`. The scans below are
heuristic screening layered on top of that boundary, never a substitute for it.
`--ignore-scripts` does NOT disable pnpm's own `.pnpmfile.cjs` hooks, so their
presence is a finding in its own right unless disclosed here. `onlyBuiltDependencies`
is pnpm 10's opt-back-in for lifecycle scripts and is likewise a finding unless
disclosed. Both lists are empty: contentus runs no install-time code.
Binds the two greater channels to each other and to a named release, rather than
to a shape. A 40-hex-shaped ref is not evidence of anything: every commit in every
repository is 40 hex. `vendored_ref` is the greater-components commit the
greater-v0.11.9 vendoring came from, recorded at the M1 `greater add` run.
Both values move together at a CLI pin bump and only through the CLI.
`cli_version` is the version string the CLI must print; a digest-verified install
at any other version FAILS SEC-7 rather than reporting on a tree it does not match.
`cli_asset` is the provenance of the tool itself. The CLI is not on the npm
registry, so nothing about the downloaded bytes is checked by a package manager,
and `--version` is the tool describing itself — any executable can print `0.11.9`
and emit a plausible doctor document. The installer verifies this digest before
unpacking and SEC-7 re-verifies it at gate time. A PATH `greater` is not accepted
at all: unverifiable provenance is BLOCKED, never PASS.
Least-privilege GitHub Actions permissions. Every workflow must declare an
explicit top-level `permissions:` block, and every scope in it — top-level or
job-level — must be `read` or `none`, except the exact write grants listed here.
CodeQL's `security-events: write` is the one exception: uploading a SARIF result
requires it, and the alternative is not running CodeQL.
`allowed_install_invocations` is the exact set of package-manager installs any
workflow — or any local composite action a workflow reaches — may run. The whole
supply-chain claim rests on `--ignore-scripts`, and the rubric can only ever fix
its own install: the workflow installs run before the rubric starts, so dropping
the flag from one of them executes dependency lifecycle code and the rubric then
reports green on the tree that code produced. The greater CLI no longer appears
here because it installs through `node gov-infra/verifiers/install-greater-cli.mjs`,
which verifies the release-asset digest first and passes `--ignore-scripts` itself.
`pinned_run_scripts` is what makes the workflow scanner's appearance rule usable.
Event-derived data may appear in a `run:` script in two shapes only: argv to a
script pinned below, or an argument to printf after a literal format. Everything
else is a finding — `bash -c`, a `<(…)` operand, a heredoc body, a `read` carrier,
the argv of any command that is not one of these scripts. Four rounds of naming
execution positions each lost to a shell spelling they had not enumerated, so the
rule stopped asking what a position would do.
The pin is the allowance. A script whose file is missing, is a symlink, or does not
hash to the value below is not in the verified set, and a `run:` handing event data
to it is judged as an ordinary command — a finding. That is also what binds the
behaviour these two workflows used to spell out inline: `main-guard`'s three `test`
comparisons and DCO's commit walk are now content-bound here rather than matched as
command text, while MAI-4 still binds the exact invocation in the workflow.

allowed_write_permissions.reason: github/codeql-action/analyze uploads SARIF to the security-events API.
